articles.title: 133,334 Projections for 66,667 Receipts
articles.description: A Count() I added for a log line was re-running my whole LINQ query. I made the projection count itself to catch the double enumeration, then fixed it in one line.
articles.body_html:
A reporting method on a dashboard endpoint started showing up in the traces twice as heavy as the numbers it returned could explain. It pulled a filtered set of orders, logged how many there were, then summed them. Two cheap-sounding operations. The profiler disagreed, and the line it kept landing on was the one I'd never have circled: a Count() call I'd added for a log message.

Here's the shape of what I had.

void Report(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} receipts", receipts.Count());

    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in receipts)
        total += r.Total;

    logger.LogInformation("Total {Total:C}", total);
}

Looks like it touches the data twice, which it does, but that's not the expensive part. The expensive part is where receipts came from. It wasn't a list. It was a LINQ pipeline someone handed down the call chain:

var receipts = orders
    .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
    .Select(o => new Receipt(o.Id, double.Parse(o.RawAmount) * 1.2));

That expression doesn't contain any receipts. It's a recipe for producing them, and it produces them fresh every single time something enumerates it. Count() enumerates it once to count. The foreach enumerates it again to sum. Same recipe, run top to bottom twice, filter and parse and allocate on both passes. The log line I thought was free was re-running the entire query.

Making the query admit it

I didn't want to argue from the profiler's vibe, so I made the projection count itself. Every time the Select runs, it bumps a counter. If the pipeline runs twice, the counter can't hide it.

int projected = 0;

IEnumerable<Receipt> Pipeline(IEnumerable<Order> orders) =>
    orders
        .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
        .Select(o =>
        {
            Interlocked.Increment(ref projected);
            var amount = double.Parse(o.RawAmount);
            return new Receipt(o.Id, amount * 1.2);
        });

Then I ran the two-pass consumer against it and compared it to the obvious fix: enumerate once into a List, then ask the list whatever you want. Two hundred thousand source rows, a third of them in the EU bucket, so 66,667 matches. Best of seven, JIT warmed first. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I trust the projection count (it's exact) more than the millisecond.

// two passes: Count() then foreach, straight off the pipeline
var count = receipts.Count();
double total = 0;
foreach (var r in receipts) total += r.Total;

// one pass: materialize, then count and sum the list
var list = receipts.ToList();
double total = 0;
foreach (var r in list) total += r.Total;

Source rows:        200,000
EU rows (expected): 66,667
Results agree:      True (66,667 receipts)

enumerate twice  projections:    133,334   best:    12.2 ms
materialize once projections:     66,667   best:     7.2 ms

Projection ratio: 2.00x
Time ratio:       1.69x

Exactly double. 133,334 projections to produce 66,667 receipts, because every receipt got built, filtered, and parsed twice and half of them thrown away the first time around. The wall clock didn't quite double, which is the honest part: parsing and allocating are most of the cost here but not all of it, so the second pass adds about two-thirds again rather than a clean 100%. The ratio you'll see depends entirely on how heavy your Select is. Mine's a double.Parse. If yours hits a database, "twice" stops being a benchmark curiosity and becomes two round trips.

The fix is one call, and so is the trap

Materializing with ToList() collapses it back to one pass. The consumer can count the list, enumerate the list, index into the list, all for free, because a List<T> is results, not a recipe. If a method is going to look at a sequence more than once, it should own a materialized copy rather than a lazy expression it doesn't control.

The caveat, and it's a real one: ToList() is also how you turn a lovely streaming, bounded-memory pipeline into a full buffer in RAM. If the sequence is huge, or infinite, or you're deliberately streaming it so you never hold all of it at once, materializing is the bug and single-pass enumeration is the feature. The honest rule I land on is about intent. If I'm going to touch a sequence exactly once, left to right, I leave it lazy. The moment a method both counts and iterates, or iterates twice, I either materialize at the top or change the signature to demand a materialized type and push the decision to the caller.

That second option is the one I actually reach for in library-ish code:

void Report(IReadOnlyCollection<Receipt> receipts)   // not IEnumerable
{
    logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} receipts", receipts.Count);
    // ...
}

IReadOnlyCollection<T> has a Count property, no enumeration required, and the type itself tells every caller "I'm going to treat this as a finished collection." You stop guessing whether the thing you were handed is a list or a time bomb, because the parameter won't accept the time bomb.

Here's the complete runnable sample if you want to watch the counter tick. Drop it in a net10.0 console project and dotnet run -c Release.

using System.Diagnostics;

Order[] source = BuildOrders(200_000);

int _projected = 0;

IEnumerable<Receipt> Pipeline(IEnumerable<Order> orders) =>
    orders
        .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
        .Select(o =>
        {
            Interlocked.Increment(ref _projected);
            var amount = double.Parse(o.RawAmount);
            return new Receipt(o.Id, amount * 1.2);
        });

static (int count, double total) SummarizeTwice(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    var count = receipts.Count();          // pass one
    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in receipts)            // pass two
        total += r.Total;
    return (count, total);
}

static (int count, double total) SummarizeOnce(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    var list = receipts.ToList();          // the only enumeration
    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in list)
        total += r.Total;
    return (list.Count, total);
}

const int Runs = 7;

_ = SummarizeTwice(Pipeline(source));
_ = SummarizeOnce(Pipeline(source));

_projected = 0;
var twiceProjected = 0;
var bestTwice = double.MaxValue;
(int count, double total) twiceResult = default;
for (int i = 0; i < Runs; i++)
{
    _projected = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    twiceResult = SummarizeTwice(Pipeline(source));
    sw.Stop();
    bestTwice = Math.Min(bestTwice, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    twiceProjected = _projected;
}

var onceProjected = 0;
var bestOnce = double.MaxValue;
(int count, double total) onceResult = default;
for (int i = 0; i < Runs; i++)
{
    _projected = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    onceResult = SummarizeOnce(Pipeline(source));
    sw.Stop();
    bestOnce = Math.Min(bestOnce, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    onceProjected = _projected;
}

var euCount = source.Count(o => o.Region == "EU");

Console.WriteLine($"Source rows:        {source.Length:N0}");
Console.WriteLine($"EU rows (expected): {euCount:N0}");
Console.WriteLine($"Results agree:      {twiceResult == onceResult} ({twiceResult.count:N0} receipts)");
Console.WriteLine();
Console.WriteLine($"enumerate twice  projections: {twiceProjected,10:N0}   best: {bestTwice,7:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"materialize once projections: {onceProjected,10:N0}   best: {bestOnce,7:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine();
Console.WriteLine($"Projection ratio: {(double)twiceProjected / onceProjected:F2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"Time ratio:       {bestTwice / bestOnce:F2}x");

static Order[] BuildOrders(int n)
{
    var regions = new[] { "EU", "US", "APAC" };
    var orders = new Order[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        orders[i] = new Order(i, regions[i % 3], (10 + i % 500).ToString());
    return orders;
}

record struct Order(int Id, string Region, string RawAmount);
record struct Receipt(int Id, double Total);

The one that bites in production isn't even this tidy. It's an IEnumerable<T> returned from a repository, passed through three methods, and somewhere along the way one of them calls .Any() to null-check and another does the real loop, and now your query ran twice and nobody wrote the word "twice" anywhere. What's the sneakiest double-enumeration you've found in your own code? I'd like to collect a few.

— still counting things nobody asked me to count

articles.title: I Built a Judge My AI Couldn't Influence. In 51 Runs, It Never Gave a B.
articles.description: I built an autonomous scientific discovery engine called RUMI. I let it run for up to 21 hours per...
articles.body_html:
I built an autonomous scientific discovery engine called RUMI. I let it run for up to 21 hours per question. Then I built a frozen external judge it had no way to influence, and graded 51 of its runs.

Zero A's. Zero B's. Forty-five C's. Six F's.

The finding isn't that an AI failed to discover things. The finding is exactly how its self-assessment failed, and what that means for anyone building agents that grade themselves.

What RUMI is

RUMI is a pipeline that takes a research question and searches the live literature. It builds a knowledge graph, mines gaps and anomalies, and generates hidden variables and causal mechanisms. It then runs a theory tournament, attacks its own winners adversarially, and refines them through a thirteen-stage "scientific courtroom." In its most ambitious mode, it rewrites its own source code. It's built by one person and runs in a terminal.

I ran it in full mode across eight domains: drug discovery, space astronomy, neuroscience, physics, materials science, mathematics, computer science, and general. Runs took anywhere from 20 minutes to 21 hours and 12 minutes. Each produced a structured report with papers, entities, gaps, anomalies, mechanisms, predictions, a tournament winner, and a self-assigned score.

The judge

RUMI scores itself on seven weighted dimensions (novelty, explanatory power, predictive power, falsifiability, evidence strength, mathematical rigor, simplicity) and assigns a grade from A to F. Like most self-scoring agents, it's generous.

So I wrote eval/harness.py: an external evaluator with six deterministic metrics, its own A-F scale, and a hash-chained append-only ledger so no one can quietly rewrite a past score. The engine is forbidden from touching the eval/ directory in its self-modification loop. The judge and the judged are separated by a wall.

The headline

Across 51 externally graded runs:

  • A: 0
  • B: 0
  • C: 45
  • F: 6

Mean external score: 52.0 out of 100. Mean self-score: 58.9. The engine's own report card said "B" about a dozen times. The judge said C forty-five times and F six.

The jitter

The easy reading is "the model is overconfident by about twenty points." That reading is wrong.

The average gap between self-score and external score is +1.1. On average, the engine is barely optimistic. The average hides a bimodal mess:

  • 26 of 51 runs scored themselves lower than the judge did.
  • 16 of 51 overshot the judge by 10 points or more.
  • The largest self-inflation was +38.0 (self 70.7, judge 32.7).
  • The largest self-deflation was -52.8 (self 0, judge 52.8).

The self-scorer isn't biased. It's uncalibrated: a noisy estimator with swings of 20 to 50 points and no reliable relationship to the external score. You can't use it as evidence, as a training signal, or as a stopping criterion. Self-assessment in an autonomous agent isn't a measurement. It's a narrative the agent tells about itself, and nothing in the score tells you whether that narrative is modest or wrong.

What I found when I went digging

It fetches real papers and then doesn't cite them. Each run pulls 100 to 105 papers from arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, and CrossRef, walks citation networks two hops deep, and enriches entities against about fifteen scientific APIs (UniProt, PDB, PubChem, ClinicalTrials, KEGG, Materials Project, and others). Yet the evidence_strength sub-score is 0 in all 67 scored runs, and the no_citations flag fires in all 51 externally graded runs. The reports contain no resolvable citations at all.

I checked that this isn't a detector blind spot. The harness reads summary_text from the report JSON, and 76 of the 78 run JSONs have that field. None contain a structured [N] citation. I also scanned the 60 raw .txt reports: no [N] markers, and no "References" or "Bibliography" section in any of them. I looked for other formats too. Author-year citations like (Smith, 2024) turned up zero hits in the reports I sampled. The few "et al." mentions were incidental references to well-known papers inside the narrative, not citations backing a claim. Nine JSONs contain a literal [1], but only inside prose, with no reference list for it to point to. Those are citation-shaped tokens, not citations.

I call this retrieval-reasoning dissociation. Retrieval is real and structurally upstream. Reasoning downstream is citation-free. The output looks grounded because the data is real, but the claims never touch it. It's the difference between a system that has read the literature and one that has only downloaded it.

Self-refinement is a coin flip. RUMI's --iterate mode runs the pipeline twice, analyzes its own weaknesses, and reruns. In one molecular-glue run, the score rose from 65.0 to 80.1. In another, on the same class of problem, it fell from 83.8 to 65.2. More compute on the same question helped about half the time.

Textbook science won novelty tournaments. At least six runs carried a NULL HYPOTHESIS CHECK: WARNING, which caps the score at 64. Winning theories included "ΛCDM Cold Dark Matter Halo" and "Standard ΛCDM with Peculiar Velocity Corrections." The standard cosmological model won a tournament meant to produce novel hypotheses.

Schema leaked into the narrative. One winning theory carried the literal variable name percolation_threshold_pc as its title. A raw code identifier made it all the way through to the story.

The system named its own process as a discovery. One drug-discovery run's winner was "Positive Feedback Loop in Research Focus," an abstract meta-process offered as the reason Alzheimer's candidates fail in late-stage trials.

Compute is not quality. The 21-hour-12-minute run, on a materials-science question, scored 60.6. A C. "Let it run overnight" is not a research strategy.

What this doesn't prove

I built both the engine and the judge, so this needs stating plainly.

First, "uncorrelated with the external score" means uncorrelated with my frozen six-metric judge, not with ground truth. The judge is deterministic and tamper-evident, but it is still my design. A harsh or miscalibrated judge would also produce zero A's.

Second, 51 runs across eight domains is a small, uneven sample. Of those, 48 predate the harness, so their external scores were backfilled into the archive rather than shipped inside each report.

Third, the judge's validation is thin. To check that the harness can reward good work at all, I built a synthetic control: a RUMI-shaped report with 5 real papers, [1] to [5] citations that resolve to those papers, cited claim sentences, a named winner, mechanism steps, and predictions. Through the same frozen harness it scored 68.6, a B, the first B the harness has ever produced. Its citation_validity and claim_support_rate were both 1.0, against 0 and null for RUMI. Its structure_completeness was 0.429, against about 0.14 for RUMI. So the harness does separate a well-cited, well-structured report from RUMI's output. But the control is something I constructed to fit the format, not a human-written scientific report, so it shows the judge can discriminate on citations and structure, not that its grades track scientific quality. A real human-written benchmark is the next test.

Fourth, one of the six metrics is effectively dead. score_consistency never fires on real RUMI data, because the reports store dimension scores as top-level keys (like novelty_score: 60) instead of under the sub-dicts the metric expects. The self-versus-external gaps in this article are unaffected, since they compare the two final scores directly. But the judge is running on five working metrics, not six, and I've documented the bug in the repo.

The diagnosis

The system retrieves real evidence and then narrates without it. Its self-score tracks nothing external, and its outputs look like science. Everything upstream of the gap (retrieval, graph, enrichment, computation) is real and often good. Everything downstream (claims, theories, scores) is unmoored. The engineering work lives in the gap between "looks grounded" and "is grounded."

What I got wrong along the way

I initially said the engine inflates its score by 14 to 22 points. That holds only for the top leaderboard rows. Across all 51 runs the mean gap is +1.1, with 26 runs under-reporting.

I initially said the external score ships inside every report JSON. That's the design intent, but the 48 pre-harness runs have it backfilled.

My first audit concluded "everything is theater." That applied to a small demo folder, not the real engine, which does retrieve, enrich, and verify mechanically. The failure is the disconnect, not an absence of capability.

Part two: the fix

The smallest fix I can think of is claim-citation binding at generation time. Every claim sentence in a generated theory must carry a citation index that resolves to a paper in that run's retrieved corpus. Claims without one are downgraded to "speculative" with a penalty, or removed.

The success criterion is frozen in advance: citation_validity and claim_support_rate must exceed 0.8 on the same topics, without degrading novelty_vs_archive or structure_completeness, as measured by the same harness. I'll publish the before and after, whichever way it goes. If it works, the pattern applies to any agent that narrates from retrieved data without citing it.

Reproduce it

Everything is open.

  • Engine: github.com/subhansh-dev/rumi
  • Dataset, frozen judge, ledger, and paper: github.com/subhansh-dev/rumi-public

Run it:

git clone https://github.com/subhansh-dev/rumi
cd rumi
python run_discovery.py "your research topic" --mode full

Reproduce a score:

cd rumi-public/Engine
python -m eval.harness ../Dataset/discovery_v2_<timestamp>.json

No API keys are included, and free-tier providers are documented in Engine/api_keys.md. The 86 eval tests pass and the ledger is hash-chained. If you find a flaw in the measurement, open an issue. That's the point.

articles.title: Embedding Fonts So a PDF Looks the Same on Every Machine
articles.description: Four families, eight faces, two renderers and one CSS quirk: what it took to stop a generated report depending on whatever fonts the server happened to have.
articles.body_html:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

The requirement was one sentence

A report generator has to produce a document that looks the same everywhere:
Chinese headings in a serif, Chinese body text in a sans, Latin headings and
cover numerals in a display serif, Latin body text and tables in Inter.
Weights matter — medium for emphasis, semibold for headings — across three
languages and two PDF renderers.

And the fonts must travel with the document. Not "the server has them
installed", not "the reader probably has them" — embedded, so a print
shop in another country sees the same pages.

The old pipeline failed on the last clause in a way that was invisible: it
depended on fonts installed on the server by a package manager, and it only
ever embedded a single CJK face. The second weight did not exist, so "bold"
was the renderer's synthetic approximation, and the only way to notice was
to open the PDF and look at what was actually inside it.

Rule one: read the fonts back out of the finished PDF

"Embedded" is a claim about the output, so I measured the output. The same
document, rendered before and after:

before after
zh page count 23 23
en page count 28 29
bm page count 30 30
fonts actually embedded one CJK face + Roboto Source Han Serif Medium + SemiBold · Source Han Sans Regular + Medium · Cormorant Garamond Medium + SemiBold · Inter Regular + SemiBold + Medium · Source Han Sans for the CJK runs inside Latin reports
render time / peak memory baseline same order (±10%, noise)
file size baseline roughly +3%

The glyph counts per face are the receipt: in the Chinese report, 15,988
glyphs land in the body sans, 2,247 in its medium weight, 634 in the heading
serif medium, 222 in its semibold. That is the difference between "the font
is on the server" and "the font is in the file" — a reader in another
country sees the same four faces, and a page count that moved by exactly one
page in one language (the Latin metrics are wider than what they replaced)
is the honest cost.

Rule two: static instances only, and the reason is in the parser

The obvious modern choice — ship one variable font per family — is wrong
here, for two measured reasons:

  1. The PDF engine's font parser reads glyf/loca only. Feed it an OpenType file with PostScript/CFF outlines and it refuses: Fonts with postscript outlines are not supported. A variable font is not the problem; CFF outlines are.
  2. It does not read the fvar table at all, so a variable font silently resolves to its default instance — and the default instances of the CJK families are the thinnest ones (Thin 100 and ExtraLight 200, visible in the name table). Every page would render in a hairline weight, with no error anywhere in the pipeline.

So the build step takes the upstream variable fonts and instantiates
static cuts: it runs the instancer, then rewrites name,
OS/2.usWeightClass and head.macStyle so the file identifies itself as
the weight it now is (the source's own name still says "Thin"). A manifest
records family, weight class, sha256, glyph count and code-point count for
every file, and the licence files ship next to them.

Rule three: the engine speaks two weights, so map onto two slots

The renderer's CSS handling honours exactly normal and bold — its source
says so in as many words ("Does not support: bolder, lighter, 100..900").
Numeric weights are therefore meaningless to it, while the headless-Chromium
renderer in the same pipeline honours them properly.

The mapping that works: each family declares an R slot and a B slot
(regular-ish and heavier), font-weight: 500 lands on the R slot of the
intended family, and 600 is rewritten to bold on the PDF side only,
which lands on the B slot. Chromium keeps 600 as written. Two tests pin
it: the B slot must be heavier than the R slot (read from usWeightClass,
not assumed), and font-weight: 600 must never appear in the stylesheet
handed to the PDF engine.

One subtlety worth the paragraph: a "medium" weight is not an emphasis
mechanism in this pipeline, it is a family member. Chinese headings use
the serif's medium as their regular and its semibold for emphasis; Latin
headings do the same with the display serif. Getting that wrong is invisible
on a screen and obvious in print.

Rule four: do not subset against a character set you do not control

The first attempt subset the CJK fonts to the union of two national
character sets and produced a ~29 MB bundle instead of ~50 MB. Then I ran
the name probe and found these were cut:

犇  骉  頔  祎  廸  玧  祾  赟  堃

Every one of them is a real given name character. The report prints a
customer's name on the cover, and the name is free input — so a subset-based
build will eventually put a tofu box on the most prominent page of the
product. Full coverage means keeping ~31k code points — roughly 50 MB of static font assets in the repository (adding only ~3% to each finished PDF after engine subsetting); that is a fine price for never showing a customer an empty rectangle.

Rule five: make missing glyphs a build failure, not a surprise

The gate runs three checks and exits non-zero on any of them:

  • every font file declared in the manifest is present, and its sha256 matches the file on disk;
  • every character in the content library (all three languages) plus the brand strings, plus probe classes — simplified, traditional, CJK punctuation, full-width forms, mixed-script, digits, Latin extended, symbols — plus the name characters, has a glyph in the face that will actually print it;
  • the lookup uses the PDF engine's own font parser rather than a third-party library, so the check cannot disagree with the renderer.

The known edges are written down instead of hidden. Dingbats and emoji (✅ ✔)
exist in none of these text fonts and the engine cannot draw colour emoji,
so they are kept out of the report body. The display serif has only 974
glyphs and does not draw symbols like ① ★ ℃, which is why the
content-library check covers all slots rather than just the body. And CJK
characters inside a Latin report must go through the dedicated CJK slot —
two tests keep the renderers from disagreeing about that.

What I would do differently

  1. Choose faces and weights before styling anything. Retrofitting a second weight after the layout exists means re-checking every page count by hand.
  2. Read the renderer's source before choosing a font format. The variable-font decision looked like a taste question and was actually a parser question — two files settled it in ten minutes.
  3. Treat everything you ship inside a document as a licence artifact. Font files enter the repo with their licences, or they enter someone else's legal review.
  4. Measure what got embedded. Page count, glyph-per-face counts, file size, render time: all four moved, and three of them moved in ways I would have guessed wrong.

The result

Before: one CJK face and a UI font, with synthetic bold, depending on what
the server had installed. After: four families and eight static faces
embedded in the file, weights that are real members of their families, page
counts within one page of the previous layout, and a lint gate that fails
the build when a character has no glyph — so the failure mode moved from "a
customer sees a box" to "CI refuses the release". Which is the same trade as
everywhere else in this pipeline: make the mistake impossible to ship rather
than easy to notice.

I build automated document generation and multi-lingual PDF publishing pipelines — from layout engine customisation and compliant font embedding to CI visual verification gates. If your business reports, invoices, or client deliverables need to look identical on every machine, get in touch: WhatsApp +60 12-797 2969 · me@hoelee.com · hoelee.com.
