articles.title: Turning Video into Line Art in the Browser with WebGL 2 and Sobel
articles.description: Depth maps and line art preserve different parts of a video. Depth describes spatial relationships;...
articles.body_html:
Depth maps and line art preserve different parts of a video. Depth describes spatial relationships; contours emphasize shape, composition, and visible changes in pose.

After adding depth-video conversion to Timeline Studio, my open-source browser video editor, I added a line-art asset generator. This version runs locally with WebGL 2 and Sobel edge extraction. It does not download or run a neural line-art model.

Source code · Try the editor

Here is how the image-processing pipeline connects to actual video editing: previews, trimmed clips, speed curves, source audio, encoding, and cancellation.

Two passes on the GPU

The pipeline is deliberately small:

Image or decoded video frame
          |
   Grayscale + 3x3 smoothing
          |
   Intermediate GPU texture
          |
   Sobel + soft threshold
          |
    Output canvas
          |
      PNG or WebM

The smoothing pass renders into a texture attached to a framebuffer. The edge pass samples that texture and draws to the output canvas. Intermediate pixels stay on the GPU rather than being read back into JavaScript between passes.

Shader programs, buffers, textures, and the framebuffer are reused across frames. That reduces setup work, although decoding and encoding still contribute to total processing time.

Convert to luminance, then smooth

The shader computes a weighted RGB luminance:

float gray(vec2 p) {
  return dot(
    texture(source, p).rgb,
    vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)
  );
}

The first pass uses this weighted 3x3 kernel, divided by 16:

1  2  1
2  4  2
1  2  1

Smoothing suppresses some high-frequency texture before edge extraction. It is a tradeoff: small details can also become weaker.

Because detection operates on luminance, different colors with similar luminance may produce weak boundaries. Conversely, a shadow or reflection can produce a strong edge without marking an object boundary.

Extract Sobel gradients

The second pass estimates horizontal and vertical gradients:

Gx                  Gy
-1  0  1            -1 -2 -1
-2  0  2             0  0  0
-1  0  1             1  2  1

Their combined magnitude becomes the edge strength:

float gradient = length(vec2(
  c + 2.0 * f + i - a - 2.0 * e - g,
  g + 2.0 * h + i - a - 2.0 * b - c
));

The letters represent neighboring luminance samples. Each output pixel performs the same local calculation, which maps naturally to a fragment shader.

Make the parameters useful

The inspector exposes detail, line weight, and inversion. Defaults are 55% detail, 1x line weight, and black lines on white.

Detail maps to an edge threshold:

float threshold = mix(0.42, 0.035, detail / 100.0);
float ink = smoothstep(threshold * 0.5, threshold, gradient);
float value = inverted ? ink : 1.0 - ink;

Higher detail lowers the threshold, retaining weaker edges. The soft threshold avoids an abrupt binary transition around the cutoff. For busy footage, increasing detail can make the result less useful by retaining background texture.

Line weight changes the sampling distance. It uses the longest dimension as a 1080px reference:

const scaledThickness =
  thickness * Math.max(width, height) / 1080;

This helps keep the edge-sampling scale comparable across output sizes. It is not morphological dilation: changing the sampling distance also changes which details respond. The initial blur itself remains a one-pixel 3x3 neighborhood.

Preview and asset generation share one renderer

Both paths call the same implementation:

const renderer = createLineArtRenderer(canvas, width, height);
renderer.draw(media, options);
// Release resources when finished:
renderer.dispose();

The preview redraws a sampled frame when parameters or the local playhead time change. Asset generation traverses output frames through that same renderer.

Sharing the implementation reduces differences in thresholds, sampling, and inversion between preview and generated assets. It does not make processing instantaneous.

Output dimensions preserve aspect ratio, cap the longest edge at 1080 by default, avoid enlarging smaller media, and normalize dimensions to even numbers.

Video has to follow the timeline's clock

A selected clip may already be trimmed or retimed. Sampling the original file from zero would produce the wrong result.

There are separate coordinates for output time, clip-local time, and source-media time. For constant speed:

sourceTime = sourceIn + clipLocalTime * speed

For speed curves, the implementation reuses the editor's mapping:

getVisualSourceTime(segment, localTime)

The generator outputs 24 fps. Each local sample time is i / 24; it is mapped to source time before decoding the frame. The processed frame is then encoded at its output timestamp.

Output frame time
       |
Source-time mapping, including trim and retiming
       |
Decode source frame -> draw contours -> encode output

Mediabunny handles media input and timestamp-based canvas sampling. The final frame duration is limited to the remaining clip duration.

24 fps is the output rate, not a claim of real-time generation speed. Actual throughput depends on the browser, hardware, source media, and encoder.

Normalize still-image orientation

One integration detail had nothing to do with Sobel: image orientation.

The image path decodes a Blob to an ImageBitmap, then draws it to a 2D canvas before uploading it to WebGL. ImageBitmap does not follow the same UNPACK_FLIP_Y_WEBGL behavior as the other upload path, so the intermediate canvas normalizes orientation.

Without that step, still images and video frames could disagree about which side is up.

Encode a reusable asset, with corresponding source audio

Images become PNG. Videos become WebM using VP9 at approximately 4 Mbps. When corresponding source audio exists, the output uses Opus at 192 kbps.

Audio preparation reuses the editor's source-audio and offline-mixing helpers so trimming and retiming follow the selected segment. This preserves the segment's corresponding source sound; it does not mix every music and narration track from the whole project.

The completed asset goes to My assets. It is not automatically inserted into the timeline, making it possible to retain the original and compare versions before placement.

Cancellation includes cleanup

An AbortController carries cancellation through source reading, frame processing, and output finalization. The renderer releases its textures, framebuffer, shaders, programs, and vertex buffer. Media input resources are disposed, and encoding is canceled when necessary.

Frame processing reports progress up to 99%. Finalization and the asset commit must finish before the UI reports completion. Processing the last frame is not the same as having a usable saved file.

What structural reference means here

Depth video and contour video provide complementary reference assets:

Asset Emphasizes
Depth video Relative depth and foreground/background layout
Line-art video Visible contours, composition, and changes in shape

A downstream generation workflow can use these only if it accepts the corresponding conditioning input and its preprocessing, timing, resolution, and frame-rate requirements are satisfied.

This feature creates the reference asset. It does not imply automatic integration with every image or video generator, nor guarantee that a generator will preserve the desired structure.

The current Sobel route also lacks semantic simplification and explicit temporal tracking. Fine textures, noise, and motion can make lines fluctuate across frames. A learned line-art model or additional temporal processing would need separate evaluation rather than being claimed as part of this implementation.

Try it or read the code

Open Effects -> Line art, select an image or video clip, adjust parameters, and generate the asset. The feature includes 13 interface languages and a mobile layout.

Implementation entry points:

  • src/lib/lineArt.js: renderer, source sampling, encoding, and cleanup
  • src/components/LineArtPanel.jsx: preview, controls, and job state
  • src/i18nLineArt.js: localized copy

If you work on browser graphics or video tools, I would welcome difficult examples: busy backgrounds, small contours, and fast motion are particularly useful for understanding where this approach needs improvement.

GitHub repository · Open the editor

Disclosure: I maintain the project discussed here. This article was drafted by an AI assistant using the current repository source and implementation notes.

articles.title: Late Chunking in Node: Embed the Whole Document, Then Cut, So 'Its' Still Means Berlin
articles.description: Naive chunking forgets what 'its' refers to. Late chunking embeds the whole document, then pools per chunk. Rebuilt in Node with Transformers.js.
articles.body_html:
• Book: AI That Reads
  • The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Take three sentences about Berlin, the same three Jina AI used to introduce late chunking:

  1. "Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany, both by area and by population."
  2. "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city, as measured by population within city limits."
  3. "The city is also one of the states of Germany, and is the third smallest state in the country in terms of area."

Split them into one chunk per sentence, embed each chunk on its own, and score each one against the query "Berlin". In Jina's run the cosine similarities came out at 0.849, 0.708 and 0.753. Sentences two and three are about Berlin. They just never say the word. "Its" and "The city" point back at a sentence the embedding model never saw.

Run the same three chunks through late chunking and Jina reports 0.850, 0.825 and 0.850. Same model, same chunks, same query. The only thing that changed is when the cut happens.

Why the middle chunk forgets Berlin

The usual RAG pipeline splits first and embeds second. Each chunk goes into the embedding model as a separate input, so the transformer's attention only covers the tokens inside that chunk. When the model reads "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants", the word "Berlin" is nowhere in its input. The token "its" gets a vector for a generic possessive pointing at some large place. Mean pooling averages that into the chunk vector, and the result lands closer to "big European city" than to "Berlin".

The late-chunking paper by Günther, Mohr, Williams, Wang and Xiao (first posted September 2024, revised July 2025) states the problem plainly: chunk embeddings built this way "can lose contextual information from surrounding chunks". Pronouns make a clean demo, but the same failure hits "the company", "this endpoint", "the second option", or any reference whose antecedent landed in a different chunk.


Naive chunking: each strip is embedded alone, so the middle one loses its link to the city.

Run the transformer once, cut afterwards

Most embedding models already work in two stages. The transformer turns every token into a vector that has attended to every other token in the input. Then a pooling step (mean pooling, for the Jina v2 family) collapses those token vectors into one vector for the whole input.

Late chunking moves the chunker between those two stages. Algorithm 1 in the paper's current version goes like this:

  1. Decide chunk boundaries the way you already do: fixed size, sentences, or a semantic splitter. You get character spans.
  2. Tokenize the whole document and run the transformer over all of it, or as much as fits in the context window.
  3. Convert each character span into a token span.
  4. Mean-pool the token vectors inside each token span. One vector per chunk.

Step 2 is where "Berlin" gets in. The token vectors for "its" were computed with attention over the first sentence, so they already carry the reference. Pooling them per chunk keeps that context inside each chunk vector. Jina's write-up puts it this way: late chunking "still requires boundary cues", but those cues "are used only after obtaining the token-level embeddings."

Two properties make it cheap to adopt. The abstract says the method "works without additional training" (the paper also offers an optional fine-tuning recipe on top). And the output doesn't change shape: one vector per chunk at the same dimension, so your vector store stays as it is.


Late chunking: the model reads the whole document first, and the cut happens on the token vectors.

Rebuilding it in Node with Transformers.js

Transformers.js runs ONNX models in Node and the browser. Xenova/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en is the ONNX port of jina-embeddings-v2-small-en, a 33M-parameter, Apache-2.0 model with an 8,192-token window. Its tokenizer config declares a BertTokenizer with model_max_length set to 8192.

npm i @huggingface/transformers

Setup and the document:

// late-chunk.mjs
import {
  AutoTokenizer,
  pipeline,
  cos_sim,
} from '@huggingface/transformers';

const MODEL = 'Xenova/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en';
const MAX_TOKENS = 8192;

const chunks = [
  'Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany, ' +
    'both by area and by population.',
  'Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants make it the ' +
    "European Union's most populous city, as measured " +
    'by population within city limits.',
  'The city is also one of the states of Germany, and ' +
    'is the third smallest state in the country in ' +
    'terms of area.',
];
const doc = chunks.join(' ');

const tokenizer = await AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL);
const extractor = await pipeline(
  'feature-extraction',
  MODEL,
  { dtype: 'fp32' },
);

Next, the token spans. The Transformers.js tokenizer options don't include an offset mapping like the Python tokenizers have, so this version counts tokens per chunk instead. The chunks are whole sentences joined by spaces, and a BERT tokenizer splits on whitespace before it breaks words into pieces, so tokenizing each chunk alone yields the same tokens as tokenizing the full document. The code still checks that the total token count matches what the model saw.

// Token span per chunk. Position 0 is [CLS].
function tokenSpans(chunks) {
  const spans = [];
  let cursor = 1;
  for (const text of chunks) {
    const ids = tokenizer.encode(text, {
      add_special_tokens: false,
    });
    spans.push([cursor, cursor + ids.length]);
    cursor += ids.length;
  }
  return { spans, total: cursor + 1 }; // + [SEP]
}

Now the late part. With pooling: 'none', the feature-extraction pipeline returns a tensor shaped [1, tokens, hidden], one vector per token. Pooling is a loop over a flat Float32Array:

function meanPool(data, dim, start, end) {
  const v = new Float32Array(dim);
  for (let t = start; t < end; t++) {
    const row = t * dim;
    for (let d = 0; d < dim; d++) v[d] += data[row + d];
  }
  for (let d = 0; d < dim; d++) v[d] /= end - start;
  return Array.from(v);
}

async function lateChunk(doc, chunks) {
  const { spans, total } = tokenSpans(chunks);
  if (total > MAX_TOKENS) {
    throw new Error(`${total} tokens, window is ${MAX_TOKENS}`);
  }
  const out = await extractor(doc, { pooling: 'none' });
  const [, seqLen, dim] = out.dims;
  if (seqLen !== total) {
    throw new Error(`spans cover ${total}, model saw ${seqLen}`);
  }
  return spans.map(([s, e]) => meanPool(out.data, dim, s, e));
}

And the comparison, with the naive version embedding each chunk as its own input:

async function naive(chunks) {
  const out = await extractor(chunks, { pooling: 'mean' });
  return out.tolist();
}

const q = await extractor('Berlin', { pooling: 'mean' });
const query = q.tolist()[0];
const before = await naive(chunks);
const after = await lateChunk(doc, chunks);

chunks.forEach((text, i) => {
  const a = cos_sim(query, before[i]).toFixed(3);
  const b = cos_sim(query, after[i]).toFixed(3);
  console.log(`naive ${a}  late ${b}  ${text.slice(0, 30)}`);
});

Run it with node late-chunk.mjs. I haven't run this exact script, so there's no output table here to copy. What to check is the direction: chunks two and three should climb toward chunk one. Jina's published numbers came from their own Python code, and an ONNX port won't match them to the decimal. The model page's own example shows fp32 and quantized weights already disagreeing in the third decimal (0.940 against 0.934). One deliberate difference from the paper: its Algorithm 1 folds [CLS] and [SEP] into the first and last chunk. To match that, start the first span at 0 and end the last span at total.

Does it hold beyond a three-sentence toy? Jina ran BEIR retrieval tasks with roughly 256-token chunks on the small model and published nDCG@10:

Dataset Avg doc length (chars) Naive Late No chunking
SciFact 1,498 64.20% 66.10% 63.89%
TRECCOVID 1,117 63.36% 64.70% 65.18%
FiQA2018 767 33.25% 33.84% 33.43%
NFCorpus 1,590 23.46% 29.98% 30.40%
Quora 62 87.19% 87.19% 87.19%

Quora documents average 62 characters, so each one fits in a single chunk and late chunking has nothing to add. In this table, the longer the documents, the bigger the gap. On TRECCOVID and NFCorpus, not chunking at all scored slightly higher than late chunking. Averaged over three models and four BEIR datasets, the paper reports nDCG@10 going from 52.2 to 54.0 with fixed-size boundaries and from 52.4 to 54.3 with sentence boundaries.

The 8,192-token wall

The trick only works if the document fits in one forward pass. Jina describes the v2 window of 8,192 tokens as "roughly ten standard pages of text". The model card says the model was trained at 512 tokens and uses a symmetric bidirectional variant of ALiBi to extrapolate to about 8k. That's why the code throws past MAX_TOKENS instead of letting anything truncate quietly.

For longer documents, the paper's Algorithm 2, "long late chunking", splits the token sequence into macro chunks of the maximum length, each overlapping the previous one by a set number of tokens. The overlap tokens provide context to the window but aren't reused in the output. The token vectors from all windows are concatenated, then pooled per chunk as before. The limit is still there: a chunk in window three can't see a definition that only appears in window one.

A few other costs come with it:

  • Edit one paragraph and you re-embed the whole document (or its window), because every chunk vector depends on the tokens around it.
  • You need token-level outputs. An endpoint that returns one pooled vector per input can't be late-chunked on your side. Jina's API has a late_chunking flag for jina-embeddings-v3: it concatenates your inputs and returns one embedding per input, with the total capped at 8,192 tokens per request.
  • It assumes mean pooling. Jina's follow-up post says it "can be applied to any long-context embedding model that uses mean pooling."

Late chunking vs Anthropic's contextual retrieval

Anthropic published Contextual Retrieval on September 19, 2024, about two weeks after the paper's first version. Their method sends Claude 3 Haiku the full document plus one chunk and asks for "a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document". The answer, usually 50 to 100 tokens, gets prepended to the chunk before embedding and before BM25 indexing. Anthropic measured retrieval failures (1 minus recall@20) dropping 35% with contextual embeddings, 49% when contextual BM25 is added, and 67% with reranking on top. They estimated the one-time cost at $1.02 per million document tokens, assuming 800-token chunks, 8k-token documents and prompt caching.

That is one LLM call per chunk. A corpus of 50,000 chunks means 50,000 generation calls at index time, plus more whenever documents change. Late chunking needs one forward pass of a 33M-parameter model per document, with no generation step. Jina's follow-up calls the LLM route "expensive in terms of cost, time, and storage", which is fair to weigh while remembering who wrote it.

The paper ran both on one small example (Section 4.5): a fictional financial document and a question about ACME Corp's Q2 2023 revenue growth. For the chunk "It highlighted a 3% revenue growth over the previous quarter.", naive chunking scored 0.6343, late chunking 0.8516, and contextual embeddings 0.8590. That's a single example: it shows the two methods landing close on one chunk and says nothing about a full corpus.

Contextual retrieval has real advantages. The added context is text, so it helps BM25 too, and it travels with the chunk into the prompt you send the generator. You can also tune the prompt for your domain, for example with a glossary, as Anthropic suggests. Late chunking only changes vectors: your keyword index and your LLM still see the raw "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants".

A reasonable order: if you host your own embedding model and your documents fit in 8k tokens, try late chunking first, because it costs one code change at index time. Reach for contextual retrieval when you need keyword search to benefit from the context, or when an index-time LLM bill is acceptable for your corpus size. Nothing stops you from doing both, though I haven't seen published numbers for the combination.

If this was useful

Late chunking is a small change at index time that plugs a recall leak most pipelines don't measure. AI That Reads is the book in my series about that whole layer in TypeScript: chunking, embeddings, vector search, and grounding answers in your own documents. If your retrieval looks fine in demos and misses on real questions, it's written for you.

It's book 2 of AI in TypeScript, five books from your first LLM call to agents in production: the whole series is here.

articles.title: This rate limit says 10 per minute. It let 20 through in 6 seconds.
articles.description: A rate limit of 10 requests per minute. Someone sends 10 requests at 0:57, then 10 more at 1:00.  All...
articles.body_html:
A rate limit of 10 requests per minute. Someone sends 10 requests at 0:57, then 10 more at 1:00.

All 20 get through, in under 6 seconds.

Nothing is broken. This is how the most common rate limiter works.

How a fixed window works

The simplest limiter cuts time into minutes and counts requests in each one. 12:00 to 12:01 is one window, 12:01 to 12:02 is the next. When a new minute starts, the count goes back to zero.

const counts = new Map(); // user -> { window, count }

function allow(user, now = Date.now()) {
  const window = Math.floor(now / 60_000); // which minute are we in?
  let c = counts.get(user);
  if (!c || c.window !== window) {
    c = { window, count: 0 }; // new minute, start from zero
    counts.set(user, c);
  }
  c.count++;
  return c.count <= 10;
}

(now is a parameter so you can test it with fake times.)

It's pretty much the first rate limiter everyone writes. One number per user, cheap to store, easy to explain.

Where it breaks

The counter doesn't remember what happened a second ago. It only knows which minute it is.

  • At 0:57 the first burst comes in. The count goes 1, 2, ... 10. All allowed.
  • At 1:00 the minute changes. The count resets to 0.
  • The second burst comes in. The count goes 1, 2, ... 10 again. All allowed.

So in about 6 seconds around the edge, the server got 20 requests. The limit says 10 per minute, and any 60 seconds that cover 0:57 to 1:03 have twice that.

That's the worst case: up to 2x the limit, if the timing lines up. And since every user's counter resets at the same moment, anyone who got blocked near the end of a minute retries at :00, all together.

The fix: count the last 60 seconds instead

Instead of asking "how many this minute?", ask "how many in the last 60 seconds?" every time a request comes in. This is called a sliding log. You keep the time of every allowed request and throw away the ones older than a minute.

const logs = new Map(); // user -> timestamps of allowed requests, oldest first

function allow(user, now = Date.now()) {
  const log = logs.get(user) ?? [];
  while (log.length && log[0] <= now - 60_000) log.shift(); // forget anything older than 60s
  if (log.length >= 10) return false;
  log.push(now);
  logs.set(user, log);
  return true;
}

Same traffic, switching between the two:

With the sliding log, the second burst gets rejected. The first 10 requests are still inside the last 60 seconds, so there's no room. The next request would get in at 1:57, exactly 60 seconds after the first one.

I ran both functions on the same 20 timestamps. The fixed window allows 20. The sliding log allows 10.

So why does anyone use fixed windows?

Memory. The sliding log stores a timestamp for every allowed request. For 10 per minute that's nothing. For 1,000 per hour across a million users, it can be a billion timestamps.

A fixed window is one counter per user. That's also why it's so easy in Redis: INCR a key, let it expire after a minute, done.

Most real limiters sit somewhere in between. A sliding window counter keeps just two numbers, this minute's count and last minute's, and estimates from those. A token bucket allows short bursts on purpose but caps the average rate. Both handle the edge much better without storing every request.

The fixed window is fine when the window is long, like a daily quota. Nobody minds much if a customer squeezes two days of usage around midnight. It hurts when the window is short and its job is protecting a server.

You can drag the two bursts around yourself and watch when the limit holds and when it doesn't: https://software-atlas.haiduc0147.dev/t/rate-limiting#fixed-window

articles.title: Day 3 never came. My son and I stopped racing and built a game engine.
articles.description: The father-vs-son race from Day 1 turned into a team. This is what we built.
articles.body_html:
In March, my son and I made a bet. 80 days. Build real software. Sell it. Father vs son, shipping every day.

Day 2 ended with four words:

Something has to change.

Then the posts stopped. Here's why.

The race stopped

We'd been racing each other. Breadth against depth. Me knocking on more doors, him polishing one thing until it shone.

Then we noticed something. We have different skills, and we think in different ways. What one of us lacks, the other brings.

And we'd both been making games and game engines for years. Separately.

So we stopped racing and started building together. Day 2 said we had to work smarter. This was it. Synergy turned out to be real.

What we built

Myth Engine.

Myth Engine is a game engine for 2D and 3D games. The games you make can run on the web, on desktop and on mobile. It's built with JavaScript and Babylon.js, and it uses ECS (entity component system), which makes putting a game together feel intuitive and helps games run fast.

You make games in the editor on Windows, with Visual Logic blocks, JavaScript, or both. The editor draws your level with the game's own runtime, so you see it as it will look in the game.

And games to go with it

We didn't just build the engine. We made games with it.

2D and 3D games, shooters, puzzles, platformers, worlds made of blocks and science labs, all made in Myth Engine.

Inside the editor

2D

  • Move, rotate and scale with the handles or the G, R and S keys.
  • Split screen, minimaps and cameras that follow the player, with no code.
  • Tile maps on square, isometric and hex grids.

3D

  • Blender's axes and keys: Z is up, and G, R and S move, rotate and scale.
  • Scenes built from sculpted terrain, grass, water and lights.
  • Havok physics makes objects fall, collide and tumble.

Objects built from components

Every object is built from components that you add and tune. The same Object Editor builds 2D and 3D objects.

Game rules: blocks, code, or both

Game rules are Visual Logic blocks you connect: when something happens, such as a button press, do something. Build a behavior once and attach it to as many objects as you like.

Pause the game right before any block runs, step through it, and watch each object's values change.

JavaScript works instead of blocks or alongside them, with suggestions for your project's own objects and sounds as you type. JavaScript libraries can be added from a catalog, and they're bundled into your game.

Pixel art

  • Paint layered art directly into your game.
  • Mirrored drawing, crisp pixel rotation and patterned gradients.
  • Recolor a sprite by changing its palette.

Looks and effects

Ready-made looks, from old film and Game Boy to thermal camera and comic-book print. Up to four can be combined.

Build new looks from connected blocks, or write them as code.

Particle effects in 2D and 3D, starting from presets such as fire, rain and confetti.

Worlds made of blocks

Generated worlds with hills, caves, ores and trees, and a map preview before you play. Block worlds can be built by hand too.

Sharing your game

  • Web games export as a single file or a web folder.
  • Desktop and mobile exports are projects you finish building yourself.
  • Multiplayer is built in, with a lobby and a relay server you host.

There's more in the full tour on itch.io: What Myth Engine can do.

The new scoreboard

Us
Products Myth Engine, plus the games we've made with it
Free guides Complete games, built step by step from an empty project

One column now. That's the twist.

Try it

The free version has no time limit. Exporting finished games needs the full version, which is a one-time purchase with no royalties.

  • Download the free version
  • Play the games and find the free guides
  • Come say hi on Discord

Call this Day 3. It just took a little longer than a day.

Next time: blocks or code? We settled it the family way.

articles.title: Hyperliquid JavaScript SDK quickstart for Node.js and TypeScript
articles.description: Install @siebly/hyperliquid-api, read public market data, set up a signed client on testnet and subscribe to Hyperliquid WebSocket streams.
articles.body_html:
Hyperliquid exposes two main HTTP endpoints (Info and Exchange) plus a WebSocket feed. You can call them directly, but signing, nonces, asset IDs and reconnect handling add up quickly. This quickstart walks through @siebly/hyperliquid-api, an MIT-licensed SDK for Node.js, JavaScript and TypeScript, from install to a live WebSocket subscription.

Everything below uses classes and methods exported by the package. The full reference lives in the Hyperliquid JavaScript SDK docs.

What you get

  • One RestClient for public market data, account information, orders, transfers and more.
  • A WebsocketClient with heartbeats, automatic reconnect and resubscribe.
  • A WebsocketAPIClient that mirrors the REST methods over Hyperliquid's WebSocket POST protocol.
  • TypeScript declarations for requests and responses, with dual ESM and CommonJS builds.
  • Testnet support through a single testnet: true option.

Install

The package supports Node.js 22 or newer.

npm install @siebly/hyperliquid-api

TypeScript is optional, but the type declarations make the request shapes much easier to discover in your editor.

Your first public REST call

Public Info methods need no credentials. Start by checking the exchange status, then pull mid prices and an order book:

import { RestClient } from '@siebly/hyperliquid-api';

const client = new RestClient();

async function main() {
  const status = await client.getExchangeStatus();
  console.log('Exchange status:', status);

  // AllMidsResponse is Record<string, string>: coin to mid price
  const mids = await client.getAllMids();
  console.log('Coins with a mid price:', Object.keys(mids).length);
  console.log('BTC mid:', mids['BTC'] ?? 'not listed');

  const book = await client.getOrderBook({
    coin: 'BTC',
    nSigFigs: 5,
  });

  if (book) {
    console.log('Best bid level:', book.levels[0][0]);
  }
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error('Request failed:', error);
});

The SDK uses readable get... names rather than Hyperliquid's internal request type names, so getAllMids() maps to the allMids Info request and getOrderBook() to l2Book.

You can also read any public account by address, without a key:

const user = '0x1234567890123456789012345678901234567890';

const perpSummary = await client.getPerpAccountSummary({ user });
const spotBalances = await client.getSpotBalances({ user });

Authenticated client setup

Signed methods take a private key, and that key belongs on a trusted backend only. Read it from an environment variable rather than hard-coding it:

import { RestClient } from '@siebly/hyperliquid-api';

const privateKey = process.env.HYPERLIQUID_PRIVATE_KEY;

if (!privateKey) {
  throw new Error('Set HYPERLIQUID_PRIVATE_KEY before starting.');
}

const client = new RestClient({
  privateKey,
  testnet: true,
});

const balances = await client.getBalances();
console.log('Account:', balances.user);
console.log('Spot:', balances.spot.balances);
console.log('Perpetuals:', balances.perp.assetPositions);

const openOrders = await client.getOpenOrders();
console.log('Open orders:', openOrders.length);

A few notes:

  • Use testnet first. testnet: true points the client at Hyperliquid's testnet API, so you can exercise signing and order flows without touching a real account.
  • Keep keys server-side. Never put a private key in frontend code, browser storage or a public environment variable. Public REST calls and public subscriptions are browser-safe; signed calls are not.
  • Custom signers. If you would rather not hand the SDK a raw key, the constructor also accepts a signer with a portable signTypedData implementation.

Once that works, the client exposes helpers for common order workflows. This places a post-only limit order on testnet:

const order = await client.submitLimitOrder({
  symbol: 'BTC',
  side: 'buy',
  size: '0.001',
  price: '50000',
  timeInForce: 'GTC',
});

if (order.status === 'ok') {
  console.log(order.response.data);
}

Exchange methods return an ExchangeResponse wrapper, so check status === 'ok' before reading response.data. For the full order surface, including submitOrder() with raw Hyperliquid order fields and submitMarketOrder(), see the Hyperliquid API JavaScript tutorial.

The README also documents how the SDK handles Hyperliquid referral and builder codes on orders; read that section before running anything on mainnet.

Subscribing to WebSocket streams

WebsocketClient opens connections when they are first needed, deduplicates matching subscriptions, sends heartbeats, and reconnects then resubscribes after a drop. You register listeners once and subscribe to topics separately:

import { WebsocketClient } from '@siebly/hyperliquid-api';

const ws = new WebsocketClient({ testnet: true });

ws.on('message', (event) => {
  if (event.channel === 'l2Book') {
    console.log(event.wsKey, event.data.coin, event.data.levels);
  } else if (event.channel === 'trades') {
    console.log(event.wsKey, event.data);
  }
});

ws.on('response', (event) => {
  console.log('Acknowledgement:', event.wsKey, event.channel, event.data);
});

ws.on('reconnected', ({ wsKey }) => {
  console.log('Reconnected:', wsKey);
});

ws.on('exception', ({ wsKey, event, data }) => {
  console.error('WebSocket exception:', wsKey, event ?? data);
});

const book = {
  type: 'l2Book',
  coin: 'BTC',
  nSigFigs: 5,
} as const;

const trades = { type: 'trades', coin: 'ETH' } as const;

await ws.subscribe([book, trades]);

// Later, when the feeds are no longer needed:
// await ws.unsubscribe([book, trades]);
// ws.closeAll();

subscribe() resolves once the socket is open and the request has been sent. The server's acknowledgement arrives on the response event, and data arrives on message with the upstream envelope intact plus a wsKey.

Coin identifiers such as BTC, @107 or PURR/USDC pass straight through. If you want to resolve a readable alias first, there is a helper:

const coin = await ws.nameToCoin('HYPE/USDC');
await ws.subscribe({ type: 'trades', coin });

Reconnect timing, ping interval and pong deadline are all configurable through the constructor options if the defaults do not suit your deployment.

Request and response over WebSockets

If you want the REST-style methods but over a persistent socket, WebsocketAPIClient provides the same Info and Exchange methods as RestClient:

import { WebsocketAPIClient } from '@siebly/hyperliquid-api';

const client = new WebsocketAPIClient({ testnet: true });
const mids = await client.getAllMids();
console.log(mids);
client.close();

Debugging tips

  • Pass a custom logger as the second argument to WebsocketClient to see pings, subscriptions and messages at trace level.
  • RestClient accepts Axios-compatible network options as its second argument, which lets you route requests through a local debugging proxy. Avoid logging signed /exchange bodies.
  • If Hyperliquid ships a new operation before the SDK has a typed wrapper, submitRawInfoRequest() keeps it usable in the meantime.

Next steps

  • Read the Hyperliquid JavaScript SDK docs for the overview and feature list.
  • Work through the Hyperliquid API JavaScript tutorial for Node.js, which covers perpetual and Spot orders, account streams, the WebSocket API, testnet and proxies in more depth.
  • Follow the Hyperliquid SDK quickstart guide on GitHub for complete end-to-end workflows.
  • Check Hyperliquid SDK release notes for recent changes.
  • Browse the source and examples in the sieblyio/hyperliquid-api repository, or install from npm.

Questions or bug reports are welcome on the GitHub issues tab.

articles.title: Gate.io JavaScript SDK quickstart for Node.js and TypeScript
articles.description: Install gateio-api, call Gate Spot REST endpoints, route WebSocket streams with WS_KEY_MAP, and place a TestNet order with the Siebly Gate SDK.
articles.body_html:
Gate.io's API covers Spot, Margin, Unified, Perpetual Futures, Delivery, Options and several WebSocket connections. Product routing (currency pair vs contract, settlement currency, account type, WS key) is easy to get wrong. This quickstart walks through gateio-api, an MIT-licensed Node.js and TypeScript SDK maintained under the Siebly organisation, from install to a TestNet-ready flow.

The full reference lives in the Gate JavaScript SDK docs. This post mirrors the canonical Gate API JavaScript tutorial.

What you get

  • One RestClient for public and private REST across Gate product groups.
  • A WebsocketClient for public market streams and private account streams.
  • A WebsocketAPIClient for awaitable Spot and Futures order commands.
  • Explicit routing helpers (WS_KEY_MAP, settle, account, currency_pair, contract).
  • TestNet, regional hosts and optional HTTP/WebSocket proxy support.
  • TypeScript declarations with dual ESM and CommonJS builds.

Install 

npm install gateio-api

The package is published on npm as gateio-api and developed at github.com/sieblyio/gateio-api.

Your first public REST calls

Public Spot methods need no credentials. Start with server time, pair metadata, a ticker, a short order book and recent candles:

import { RestClient } from 'gateio-api';

const client = new RestClient();

async function main() {
  const time = await client.getServerTime();
  console.log('Server time:', time.server_time);

  const pair = await client.getSpotCurrencyPair({
    currency_pair: 'BTC_USDT',
  });
  console.log('BTC_USDT metadata:', pair);

  const tickers = await client.getSpotTicker({
    currency_pair: 'BTC_USDT',
  });
  console.log('BTC_USDT ticker:', tickers[0]);

  const orderBook = await client.getSpotOrderBook({
    currency_pair: 'BTC_USDT',
    limit: 5,
  });
  console.log('Best bid:', orderBook.bids[0]);
  console.log('Best ask:', orderBook.asks[0]);

  const candles = await client.getSpotCandles({
    currency_pair: 'BTC_USDT',
    interval: '1h',
    limit: 10,
  });
  console.log('Latest candle:', candles[0]);
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error('Request failed:', error);
});

Keep product fields explicit: Spot uses currency_pair, Futures and Delivery use settle plus contract, and Spot orders that touch a specific account pass account.

Authenticated REST setup

Private methods need an API key and secret from Gate. Keep them in environment variables on a trusted backend only:

import { RestClient } from 'gateio-api';

const client = new RestClient({
  apiKey: process.env.GATE_API_KEY!,
  apiSecret: process.env.GATE_API_SECRET!,
});

const balances = await client.getSpotAccounts();
console.log('Spot balances:', balances.slice(0, 3));

For Futures, pass settle on each request (for example 'usdt'). Use a separate TestNet key when you point the client at Gate's TestNet host.

WebSocket subscriptions

Public and private streams go through WebsocketClient. Pick the connection with WS_KEY_MAP so Spot and perpetual streams do not collide:

import { WebsocketClient } from 'gateio-api';

const ws = new WebsocketClient();

ws.on('update', (data) => {
  console.log('Update:', data);
});

ws.on('exception', (err) => {
  console.error('WebSocket error:', err);
});

// Public Spot ticker stream (second arg selects the Gate WS connection)
ws.subscribe(
  { topic: 'spot.tickers', payload: ['BTC_USDT'] },
  'spotV4',
);

Private streams need the same API credentials as REST. Subscribe only after the client reports a successful auth on that connection.

WebSocket API order commands

When you want request/response style order commands over WebSocket, use WebsocketAPIClient for Spot or Futures, await the reply, then confirm final state over REST or a private fill stream. Details and examples are in the Gate tutorial.

TestNet, hosts and proxies

  • Keep live and TestNet API keys separate.
  • Select the matching baseUrl / wsUrl (or the SDK's TestNet option) before you send signed traffic.
  • Configure an HTTP(S) agent when your environment requires a proxy.

Next steps

  • Full method list and options: Gate JavaScript & TypeScript SDK
  • Step-by-step tutorial (this article's source): Gate API JavaScript Tutorial
  • npm: gateio-api
  • Source: sieblyio/gateio-api

Siebly also publishes typed SDKs for Binance, Bybit, OKX, Bitget, KuCoin, Coinbase, Kraken, HTX and Hyperliquid. See the Siebly SDK overview for the full set.

articles.title: Highlighting text without wrapping it in spans: the CSS Custom Highlight API
articles.description: The CSS Custom Highlight API is a browser API that lets you style arbitrary ranges of text by...
articles.body_html:
The CSS Custom Highlight API is a browser API that lets you style arbitrary ranges of text by registering Range objects in a Highlight, adding it to CSS.highlights under a name, and targeting that name with the ::highlight() pseudo-element. The DOM stays exactly as it was: no <span>, no <mark>, no extra nodes.

I ran into this while building a highlights-and-notes feature, and it changed how I think about the problem. This post covers why the old approach hurts, how the native API works, what support looks like today, and what you still have to build yourself.

What is wrong with wrapping highlights in spans?

For about fifteen years, the standard way to highlight text on a web page was to split text nodes and wrap the pieces in elements. mark.js wraps matches in <mark>. Rangy's highlighter and web-highlighter wrap them in <span>. It works, but it has costs:

  • You are editing a DOM someone else owns. In React, Vue or Svelte, the framework assumes it controls the nodes it rendered. If a library splits a text node and inserts a <span>, the next re-render can throw the highlight away, or fail outright when the framework tries to update a node that is no longer where it expected. If you've ever seen Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node' after a third-party script touched your markup, you know what this looks like.
  • Overlapping highlights get messy. Two highlights that partly overlap need nested or split wrappers, and removing one means stitching text nodes back together correctly.
  • Selectors and styles change. p > a or :first-child can stop matching once extra elements appear. Copy and paste, textContent offsets and screen readers can all pick up the new structure.
  • Cleanup is your problem. Every "remove highlight" has to unwrap and normalize the nodes, or the DOM slowly fills with fragments.

None of this is a bug in those libraries. When they were written, wrapping was the only way to paint text.

How does the CSS Custom Highlight API work?

There are three pieces:

  1. Range: the same DOM Range you get from document.createRange() or new Range(), with a start and end inside text nodes.
  2. Highlight: a set-like object that holds one or more ranges.
  3. CSS.highlights: a registry (a HighlightRegistry, which behaves like a Map) where you give each Highlight a name. CSS then styles that name with ::highlight(name).

Here is the minimal version, with no library:

<p id="intro">The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.</p>

::highlight(note) {
  background-color: #fde68a;
  color: inherit;
}

if (typeof CSS !== 'undefined' && 'highlights' in CSS) {
  const textNode = document.getElementById('intro').firstChild;

  const range = new Range();
  range.setStart(textNode, 4);  // start of "quick"
  range.setEnd(textNode, 19);   // end of "fox"

  const highlight = new Highlight(range);
  CSS.highlights.set('note', highlight);

  // Later, to remove it:
  // CSS.highlights.delete('note');
}

Open DevTools after running this: the <p> still has a single text node. The browser paints the range, but nothing in the tree changed, so React (or anything else) can re-render the paragraph and the highlight is still painted as long as the range points at live nodes.

A few things the spec deliberately limits:

  • Only some properties apply inside ::highlight(): color, background-color, text-decoration and its longhands, text-shadow, and a handful of others. No padding, no border, no layout changes. That is the point: painting, not layout.
  • Ranges are live. If the DOM under a range changes, the range moves or collapses with it. That's great for small edits and a problem when a framework replaces the whole node (more on that below).
  • Highlights are not elements, so they get no events. There's no click on a highlight. You hit-test yourself: get the caret position from the pointer with document.caretPositionFromPoint() and check which range contains it, or compare the pointer against range.getClientRects(). A newer CSS.highlights.highlightsFromPoint() does this for you, but support is still partial (see below).
  • Priority. When highlights overlap, highlight.priority decides which one paints on top.

Which browsers support the CSS Custom Highlight API?

Checked on 3 November 2026 against MDN's browser-compat-data and the web-features "Custom highlights" entry:

Browser Highlight / CSS.highlights ::highlight() styling
Chrome / Edge 105 (2022) 105
Safari (macOS and iOS) 17.2 (December 2023) 17.2
Firefox 140 partial from 140 to 148: text-decoration works from 146, text-shadow from 149. Full from 149

The feature became Baseline "newly available" on 24 March 2026, when Firefox 149 shipped full ::highlight() support. Two caveats worth knowing:

  • In Safari, ::highlight() styles are ignored on text that also has user-select: none.
  • CSS.highlights.highlightsFromPoint() is only in Chrome 140+ and Firefox 150+ (Safari has it in preview), so keep a manual hit-test fallback.

If you need to support older browsers, there is no polyfill that keeps the "no DOM changes" property. You either fall back to wrapping, or you simply don't show highlights there.

What do you still have to build yourself?

The native API paints ranges. That's all it does. For a real highlights-and-notes feature, you still need:

  • Persistence. A Range is a pair of node references. It can't be saved to localStorage or a database. You need to serialize it into something stable.
  • Re-anchoring. When the page loads again, or the content was edited, or a framework re-rendered and replaced the text nodes, you have to find the text again and build fresh ranges. Character offsets alone break as soon as one word changes above your highlight.
  • Selection UI. Turning a user's selection into a highlight, and showing a toolbar or note editor next to it.
  • Hit-testing, as above, to open the note when someone clicks a highlight.
  • Framework lifecycle. Creating and destroying everything when a component mounts and unmounts, and not running on the server during SSR.

How does penciled build on top of it?

This is the part where I talk about my own project. I wrote penciled (penciled.org, JavaScript highlights & notes library), an MIT-licensed library of about 15 kB that does the list above on top of the Custom Highlight API. It never inserts elements into your content, and it has no wrapping fallback.

The default setup, with a built-in toolbar and note editor:

import { annotate } from 'penciled';
import 'penciled/styles.css';

const penciled = annotate('#article', {
  documentId: 'my-post',
  storage: 'local', // or 'memory', or your own adapter with load/save
});

const off = penciled.on('create', (annotation) => {
  console.log('created', annotation);
});

What it handles:

  • Persistence: localStorage by default, or a custom storage adapter (an object with load and save, plus optional create, update and delete) to sync with your backend. export() and import() move annotations around, and toW3C() converts them to the W3C Web Annotation format.
  • Anchoring: each annotation stores the quoted text, a short prefix and suffix, and start/end positions. On load, penciled tries the stored position, then exact matches of the quote, then a fuzzy match, and only accepts a result above a confidence threshold. If the text really is gone, the annotation isn't silently painted in the wrong place. It's marked as an orphan, fires an orphan event and stays in storage.
  • Notes: each highlight can carry a note, with a color and an indicator for highlights that have notes.
  • React: penciled/react exports an <Annotatable> component and a useAnnotations() hook. It's SSR-safe, because the instance is only created in an effect, and React can re-render the annotated content as often as it likes: 
import { Annotatable } from 'penciled/react';
import 'penciled/styles.css';

export function Post({ post, children }) {
  return (
    <Annotatable as="article" options={{ documentId: post.id }}>
      {children}
    </Annotatable>
  );
}
  • Headless: penciled/headless (about 6 kB) is the same engine without the UI. You get select events with the selected range and build your own toolbar: 
import { annotate } from 'penciled/headless';

const penciled = annotate('#article');

penciled.on('select', (context) => {
  if (!context || context.annotation || !context.editable) return;
  // position your own button using context.range.getBoundingClientRect()
  // then: penciled.create(context.range, { color: 'yellow' });
});

Highlights are registered as named highlights (penciled-<color>, penciled-<color>-noted, penciled-active), so you can style them with ordinary ::highlight() rules.

How does it compare to mark.js, Rangy and other options?

Honestly, it depends on what you need. These numbers come from my own comparison page, measured on 22 October 2026 (sizes are min+gzip):

Library How it paints Size Notes
mark.js wraps in <mark> ~6.2 kB Built for search-term highlighting, not saved annotations. Last release 8.11.1 in January 2018, still ~1.9M weekly downloads.
Rangy wraps in <span> ~22.7 kB A broad range/selection toolkit with a highlighter module. Latest 1.3.2.
web-highlighter wraps in <span> ~9.4 kB Persistence-oriented, and works back to IE11, which the native API can't.
@recogito/text-annotator separate overlay layer ~22.4 kB BSD-3, W3C annotation model, strong for collaborative and scholarly annotation.
Annotator.js jQuery-based — Last released in 2015. Hypothesis was originally built on it.
penciled CSS Custom Highlight API ~15 kB (~6 kB headless) No DOM changes, persistence and fuzzy re-anchoring built in. Pre-1.0, with far fewer users (~640 weekly downloads).

My rough guide:

  • Highlighting search matches on a static page? mark.js is small and battle-tested.
  • Need IE11 or very old browsers? You need a wrapping library such as web-highlighter or Rangy.
  • Collaborative, shared annotation with accounts and groups? Look at Hypothesis or Recogito.
  • Persistent personal highlights and notes in a modern app, especially one rendered by React, where you can't let a library rewrite your markup? That's the case I built penciled for.

If you only need to paint a few ranges, you don't need any library. The ten lines of native code above are enough.

Where can I try it?

Docs and a live demo are at penciled.org, and the source is on GitHub. There's also a free browser extension for Chrome, Firefox and Edge built on the same library, if you just want to highlight pages you read.

I'm Marcel Losso, the creator and maintainer of penciled, so weigh my comparison accordingly. Corrections and issues are very welcome on GitHub.

articles.title: Why I used a CRDT and not OT for a collaborative editor
articles.description: I built Synapse to see if I could make two people edit the same paragraph offline, reconnect, and...
articles.body_html:
I built Synapse to see if I could make two people edit the same paragraph offline, reconnect, and lose nothing. This is what I learned about CRDTs along the way, including two things I got wrong.

Why not OT

Operational transformation needs a server to put every edit in order and rewrite late ones. That works, but it means a client that was offline for 20 minutes comes back with a pile of old edits the server has to rebase. I did not want my design to depend on that, so I used Yjs, which is a CRDT. Every character has an identity, so copies can merge in any order and end up the same.

The first thing I got wrong

I wrote a small script where two people type at the same spot while offline, then I sent their edits to two observers in opposite orders. I expected the arrival order to decide the result. It did not. Both observers ended with the same text. Yjs breaks the tie using each copy's client ID, and every copy compares the same IDs. I only understood this when I set the IDs by hand and flipped the result by flipping the IDs.

The second thing I got wrong

My compaction code saved a snapshot and then deleted every edit up to number N. Under a test that wrote from two places at once, edits went missing. An edit gets its number before it is saved, so compaction could read "up to 10" while edit 8 was still being written, and then delete it.

The fix was not a lock. Applying the same Yjs update twice changes nothing, so loading can merge everything it finds, duplicates included, and compaction only deletes the exact records it read. Two compactions at once can no longer lose data. A property of the data type replaced a coordination protocol, and that is why I trust the choice.

What it costs

Documents get bigger than their text, because every character has an identity and deleted text leaves a marker. I merge the edit log into a snapshot every 100 edits to keep it in check.

A CRDT also only guarantees that copies agree. If one person deletes a word while another types inside it, both copies agree on the result, and it may not be what either person wanted.

How I checked it

I wrote a property based test: three copies take random inserts, deletes and formatting, sync in random orders, and must end identical. It has run 10,000 times. My first version failed after 2,771 runs and I assumed I had broken convergence. I had not. The text and formatting matched. What differed was an internal record that each copy tidies up on its own schedule. So the real guarantee is identical content immediately, and identical stored bytes once syncing goes quiet. I rewrote the test to check exactly that, and it has passed every run since.

I also simulated 30 minutes of two people typing offline, about 7,200 edits each. After reconnecting, both screens agreed in 58 ms. That was one laptop with no real network, so it shows merge cost, not what a user would wait for.

Code
Repo: https://github.com/yashwanthvarmakonduru/synapse

Longer writeup with the benchmark table: https://github.com/yashwanthvarmakonduru/synapse/blob/main/docs/blog/why-a-crdt-not-ot.md
